items.item: Backfilling is the process of running partitions for assets, supported for each partition or a subset of partitions.

at.step: Reveal: chunk the history into independent pieces

items.item: By default, a backfill covering N partitions launches N separate runs, one per partition.

at.step: Reveal: chunk the history into independent pieces

items.item: Writes are performed on a separate audit-branch independent from the main table history.

at.step: Reveal: write to a shadow, then one atomic swap

items.item: The main branch can be fast-forwarded to the head of the audit branch to update the main table state.

at.step: Reveal: write to a shadow, then one atomic swap

items.item: A checkpoint resumes at the first incomplete chunk, not the start — the whole point of an idempotent chunk.

at.step: Reveal: idempotent chunks, a durable checkpoint

items.item: A throttle's signal is production's own latency, not a fixed concurrency number chosen once and left alone.

at.step: Reveal: the throttle reacts to production, not a number

items.item: The diff must show only the intended change, or the swap doesn't happen at all.

at.step: Reveal: validate with a data diff before the swap

items.item: A bigger single job still dies as one unit and still contends with production the same way, just for longer.

at.step: Predict: what four decisions prevent this?

items.item: A throttle's whole job is to react to production's live latency continuously, not to act only as a gate before the run starts.

at.step: Prove it: a throttle someone switched off

items.item: A failed backfill run is discarded, never repaired in place, because promotion is a single atomic swap that either happens or doesn't.

at.step: Reveal: write to a shadow, then one atomic swap

items.item: This topic leaves out the orchestrator's backfill mechanics, write-audit-publish and data-diff internals, the table-format branch-and-swap mechanics, idempotent writes, and concurrent-writer conflicts with live ingest.
Chunked idempotent backfills and shadow-then-swap validation are established practice, not an emerging technique.
This topic gives the shop its backfill design; the next design asks whether the pipeline needed two pieces of logic in the first place, building it both ways as Kappa and Lambda.
The real design question for a throttle isn't how many workers the budget allows, but what signal tells it to slow down.
